subject.name: Physics
subject.description: Cambridge International AS & A Level Physics. Topics 1–11 are assessed at AS Level (Papers 1 and 2) and topics 12–25 at A Level (Paper 4). Values use the constants on the Cambridge data sheet, with g = 9.81 m s⁻². You can type answers in standard form, for example 2.0e11 or 2.0 × 10^11. The practical papers (3 and 5) are not included. The questions are original practice questions written in the style of Cambridge papers, not reproduced past paper material.

topics.title: Physical quantities and units
topics.summary: SI units, estimates, scalars and vectors, errors and uncertainties.

topics.title: Kinematics
topics.summary: Equations of motion, graphs, projectile motion.

topics.title: Dynamics
topics.summary: Momentum, Newton's laws, non-uniform motion, conservation of momentum.

topics.title: Forces, density and pressure
topics.summary: Turning effects, equilibrium, density, pressure and upthrust.

topics.title: Work, energy and power
topics.summary: Energy conservation, gravitational potential and kinetic energy, efficiency, power.

topics.title: Deformation of solids
topics.summary: Stress, strain, Young modulus, elastic and plastic behaviour.

topics.title: Waves
topics.summary: Progressive waves, transverse and longitudinal waves, Doppler effect, electromagnetic spectrum, polarisation.

topics.title: Superposition
topics.summary: Stationary waves, diffraction, interference, the diffraction grating.

topics.title: Electricity
topics.summary: Charge, current, potential difference, resistance and resistivity.

topics.title: D.C. circuits
topics.summary: Kirchhoff's laws, e.m.f., internal resistance, potential dividers.

topics.title: Particle physics
topics.summary: Atomic structure, radioactive decay, fundamental particles and quarks.

topics.title: Motion in a circle
topics.summary: Angular speed, centripetal acceleration and force.

topics.title: Gravitational fields
topics.summary: Newton's law of gravitation, field strength, potential, orbits.

topics.title: Temperature
topics.summary: Thermal equilibrium, temperature scales, specific heat capacity and latent heat.

topics.title: Ideal gases
topics.summary: The ideal gas equation and the kinetic theory of gases.

topics.title: Thermodynamics
topics.summary: Internal energy and the first law of thermodynamics.

topics.title: Oscillations
topics.summary: Simple harmonic motion, energy in SHM, damping and resonance.

topics.title: Electric fields
topics.summary: Field strength, Coulomb's law, electric potential.

topics.title: Capacitance
topics.summary: Capacitors in circuits, energy stored, charging and discharging.

topics.title: Magnetic fields
topics.summary: Force on currents and moving charges, electromagnetic induction.

topics.title: Alternating currents
topics.summary: Characteristics of a.c., r.m.s. values, rectification and smoothing.

topics.title: Quantum physics
topics.summary: Photons, the photoelectric effect, wave-particle duality, energy levels.

topics.title: Nuclear physics
topics.summary: Mass defect, binding energy, radioactive decay and half-life.

topics.title: Medical physics
topics.summary: Ultrasound, X-rays, PET scanning.

topics.title: Astronomy and cosmology
topics.summary: Standard candles, stellar radii, Hubble's law and the Big Bang.

parts.prompt: Which of the following is an SI base unit?
parts.examinerComment: The newton, joule and volt are derived units. The seven base units should be learned.

parts.prompt: Which expresses the joule in SI base units?
parts.examinerComment: Work = force × distance, so J = (kg m s⁻²) × m.

parts.prompt: A ball is dropped from rest. Air resistance is negligible. How far does it fall in the first 2.0 s?
parts.examinerComment: Using s = ½gt² gives 19.6 m. Option D comes from forgetting the ½.

parts.prompt: What does the gradient of a velocity–time graph represent?
parts.examinerComment: The area under the graph gives displacement; the gradient gives acceleration.

parts.prompt: A book rests on a table. Which force forms a Newton's third law pair with the weight of the book?

options.text: the gravitational pull of the book on the Earth
the normal contact force of the table on the book
the normal contact force of the book on the table

markingPoints.text: A – the gravitational pull of the book on the Earth

parts.examinerComment: Option B was the most common answer. Third law pairs act on different bodies and are the same type of force.

parts.prompt: Which is a unit of momentum?
parts.examinerComment: Momentum change equals impulse, which is force × time.

parts.prompt: What is the pressure due to water at a depth of {h} m? (density of water = 1000 kg m⁻³)
parts.examinerComment: Δp = ρgΔh = 1000 × 9.81 × {h} = {=round(9810*h)} Pa. Candidates who chose B usually omitted g.

parts.prompt: An object is fully submerged in a liquid. What is the upthrust on the object equal to?

options.text: the pressure at the bottom of the object

markingPoints.text: B – the weight of liquid displaced

parts.examinerComment: Upthrust is a force, so it equals the weight (not mass) of the displaced liquid.

parts.prompt: A motor uses {Ein} J of electrical energy to lift a load and gives the load {=Ein*p/100} J of potential energy. What is its efficiency?
parts.examinerComment: Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input = {=Ein*p/100} ÷ {Ein}. An efficiency above 100% is impossible, so options C and D could be rejected at once.

parts.prompt: What is the kinetic energy of a mass of {m} kg moving at {v} m s⁻¹?
parts.examinerComment: Option D comes from omitting the ½ in ½mv²; options A and B forget to square the speed.

parts.prompt: Which expression defines the Young modulus?
parts.examinerComment: Option A is the spring constant; option D is stress.

parts.prompt: A force of 6.0 N extends a spring by 0.030 m. What is the spring constant?
parts.examinerComment: k = F ÷ x. Candidates should check that the extension is in metres.

parts.prompt: A wave has frequency {f} Hz and wavelength {lam} m. What is its speed?
parts.examinerComment: v = fλ.

parts.prompt: Which type of wave is longitudinal?
parts.examinerComment: All electromagnetic waves are transverse.

parts.prompt: Two coherent sources produce an interference pattern. What is the path difference at a point of maximum intensity?

options.text: any odd number of half wavelengths

markingPoints.text: B – a whole number of wavelengths

parts.examinerComment: Option D is one case of option B but not the only one.

parts.prompt: What is the distance between adjacent nodes in a stationary wave?
parts.examinerComment: Node to adjacent antinode is λ/4; node to node is λ/2.

parts.prompt: A current of {I} A flows for {t} s. How much charge passes a point?
parts.examinerComment: Q = It.

parts.prompt: Which change doubles the resistance of a wire?
parts.examinerComment: R = ρL/A. Doubling the diameter quarters the resistance.

parts.prompt: Two {R} Ω resistors are connected in parallel. What is the combined resistance?
parts.examinerComment: For identical resistors in parallel, the total is the value divided by the number of resistors. Option A is 1/R + 1/R, which candidates forgot to invert.

parts.prompt: Kirchhoff's first law is a consequence of the conservation of which quantity?
parts.examinerComment: Kirchhoff's second law follows from conservation of energy.

parts.prompt: What is an α-particle made of?
parts.examinerComment: An α-particle is a helium nucleus.

parts.prompt: What is the quark composition of a proton?
parts.examinerComment: A neutron is udd. Charges: u = +⅔e, d = −⅓e.

parts.prompt: The length of a rectangle is measured as {L} ± {dL} cm and its width as {W} ± {dW} cm. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in its area.
parts.examinerComment: Percentage uncertainties add when quantities are multiplied.

parts.prompt: A ball is thrown horizontally at {u} m s⁻¹ from the top of a cliff {h} m high. Air resistance is negligible. Calculate the horizontal distance the ball travels before hitting the ground, in m.
parts.examinerComment: Horizontal and vertical motion must be treated separately. The horizontal velocity stays constant.

parts.prompt: A constant resultant force of {F} N acts on a mass of 2.5 kg, initially at rest, for {t} s. Calculate the final momentum of the mass, in N s.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered. The mass is not needed.

parts.prompt: A weight of {W} N hangs {a} m from a pivot on a light rod. Calculate the vertical force needed {b} m from the pivot on the other side to balance the rod, in N.
parts.examinerComment: State the principle of moments when using it.

parts.prompt: A crane lifts a load of mass {m} kg vertically through {h} m in {t} s at constant speed. Calculate the useful output power of the crane, in W.

markingPoints.text: C1 for work done = mgh = {=round(m*9.81*h)} J

parts.examinerComment: Some candidates used mass instead of weight.

parts.prompt: A wire of length 2.0 m and cross-sectional area 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m² extends by {x} mm under a tension of {F} N. Calculate the Young modulus of the material, in Pa.
parts.examinerComment: Converting the extension from mm to m was essential. Answers can be typed as 2.0e11 or 2.0 × 10^11.

parts.prompt: A source emits sound of frequency {fs} Hz and moves directly towards a stationary observer at {vs} m s⁻¹. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. Calculate the frequency heard by the observer, in Hz.
parts.examinerComment: Using (v + vₛ) for an approaching source gave a frequency lower than {fs} Hz, which candidates should have recognised as wrong.

parts.prompt: In a double-slit experiment the slit separation is {a} mm, the screen is {D} m from the slits, and the fringe separation is {=round(lam*D/a/1000,2)} mm. Calculate the wavelength of the light, in m.
parts.examinerComment: Unit conversion from mm was the main source of error.

parts.prompt: A {Vs} V supply provides a current of {I} A to a heater. Calculate the energy transferred in {t} minutes, in J.

markingPoints.text: C1 for E = VIt with t = {=60*t} s

parts.examinerComment: Minutes must be converted to seconds.

parts.prompt: A battery of e.m.f. {emf} V and internal resistance {r} Ω is connected to a {R} Ω resistor. Calculate the potential difference across the resistor, in V.
parts.examinerComment: Some candidates ignored the internal resistance and gave {emf} V.

parts.prompt: Describe the change in quark composition that occurs in β⁻ decay, and name the leptons emitted.

markingPoints.text: B1 for a down quark changing into an up quark (udd → uud)
B1 for an electron and an electron antineutrino emitted

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates wrote 'neutrino' rather than 'antineutrino' for β⁻ decay.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Calculate the angular speed, in rad s⁻¹, of a wheel rotating at {n} revolutions per minute.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A car of mass {m} kg travels round a horizontal bend of radius {r} m at a constant speed of {v} m s⁻¹. Calculate the resultant force on the car, in N.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain why an object moving in a circle at constant speed is accelerating.

markingPoints.text: B1 for its velocity changes because its direction changes
B1 for the acceleration (and resultant force) is towards the centre of the circle

parts.examinerComment: Answers must refer to velocity, not speed, changing.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: The Earth has mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m. Calculate the gravitational field strength at its surface, in N kg⁻¹.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A geostationary satellite orbits the Earth (mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg) with a period of 24 hours. Calculate the radius of its orbit, in m.

markingPoints.text: C1 for GMm/r² = mω²r or r³ = GMT²/4π²

parts.examinerComment: Many forgot to convert the period to seconds.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Define gravitational potential at a point.

markingPoints.text: B1 for work done per unit mass
B1 for bringing a small test mass from infinity to the point

parts.examinerComment: Both 'per unit mass' and 'from infinity' are required.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Convert a temperature of {theta} °C to kelvin.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Calculate the energy needed to heat {m} kg of water from {t1} °C to {t2} °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Give your answer in J.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Calculate the energy needed to melt {m} kg of ice at 0 °C. The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. Give your answer in J.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A gas at a pressure of {p} × 10⁵ Pa occupies {Vg} m³ at {T} K. Calculate the amount of gas, in mol.
parts.examinerComment: Temperatures must be in kelvin.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Calculate the mean translational kinetic energy of a gas molecule at {T} K, in J.
parts.examinerComment: Answers can be typed as 6.21e-21.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: State two assumptions of the kinetic theory of gases.

markingPoints.text: B1 for molecules have negligible volume compared with the container
B1 for no intermolecular forces (except during collisions)
B1 for the time of a collision is negligible compared with the time between collisions
B1 for molecules move randomly / there are a very large number of molecules

parts.examinerComment: Statements such as 'molecules are small' were not precise enough.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A gas is supplied with {q} J of thermal energy and does {w} J of work on its surroundings. Calculate the increase in its internal energy, in J.

markingPoints.text: C1 for ΔU = q + W with W = −{w} J

parts.examinerComment: Sign conventions caused difficulty. Work done by the gas is negative in ΔU = q + W.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A gas expands at a constant pressure of {p} × 10⁵ Pa and its volume increases by {dV} m³. Calculate the work done by the gas, in J.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain what is meant by the internal energy of a system.

markingPoints.text: B1 for the sum of the random kinetic and potential energies
B1 of the molecules in the system

parts.examinerComment: Both kinetic and potential energy must be mentioned, and 'random' is required.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A mass of {m} kg on a spring of spring constant {k} N m⁻¹ oscillates with simple harmonic motion. Calculate the period, in s.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: An object performs simple harmonic motion with amplitude {x0} m and angular frequency {w} rad s⁻¹. Calculate its maximum speed, in m s⁻¹.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Define simple harmonic motion.

markingPoints.text: B1 for acceleration proportional to displacement from a fixed point
B1 for acceleration directed towards that point / in the opposite direction to displacement

parts.examinerComment: The direction of the acceleration must be stated.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Two parallel plates {d} cm apart have a potential difference of {Vp} V between them. Calculate the electric field strength, in V m⁻¹.

markingPoints.text: C1 for E = V/d with d in metres

parts.examinerComment: Converting cm to m was essential.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Two point charges of +{q1} μC and +{q2} μC are {r} m apart in a vacuum. Calculate the force between them, in N.

markingPoints.text: C1 for correct substitution with μC converted

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of {Vp} V. Calculate its kinetic energy, in J.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A {C} μF capacitor is charged to {Vc} V. Calculate the charge stored, in C.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Calculate the energy stored in a {C} μF capacitor charged to a potential difference of {Vc} V, in J.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A {C} μF capacitor discharges through a {R} kΩ resistor. Calculate the time constant, in s.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered. Both prefixes (μ and k) must be converted.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A wire of length {L} m carries a current of {I} A at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density {B} T. Calculate the force on the wire, in N.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: An electron moves at {v} × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density {B} × 10⁻³ T. Calculate the radius of its circular path, in m.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: The magnetic flux through a {N}-turn coil changes by {dF} Wb in {dt} s. Calculate the average induced e.m.f., in V.
parts.examinerComment: Some forgot to multiply by the number of turns.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: An alternating voltage has a peak value of {V0} V. Calculate its r.m.s. value, in V.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: An alternating voltage of peak value {V0} V is applied across a {R} Ω resistor. Calculate the mean power dissipated, in W.
parts.examinerComment: Using the peak voltage doubled the answer.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain how a capacitor connected across the output of a rectifier smooths the output voltage.

markingPoints.text: B1 for the capacitor charges when the output voltage rises
B1 for it discharges through the load when the voltage falls, reducing the ripple

parts.examinerComment: Good answers referred to the time constant being much longer than the period of the supply.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Calculate the energy of a photon of wavelength {lam} nm, in J.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Light with photon energy {Ep} eV falls on a metal with work function {W0} eV. Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons, in eV.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving at {v} × 10⁶ m s⁻¹, in m.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of {T} days. What fraction of the original nuclei remains after {=n*T} days?
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5730 years. Calculate its decay constant, in year⁻¹.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: In a nuclear reaction the mass decreases by {dm} u. Calculate the energy released, in J.

markingPoints.text: C1 for converting u to kg

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: An X-ray beam passes through {x} cm of tissue with linear attenuation coefficient {mu} cm⁻¹. Calculate the fraction of the intensity transmitted.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Soft tissue has density {rho} kg m⁻³ and the speed of ultrasound in it is {c} m s⁻¹. Calculate its specific acoustic impedance, in kg m⁻² s⁻¹.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain why a gel is used between the ultrasound transducer and the skin.

markingPoints.text: B1 for it removes the air between the transducer and the skin
B1 for air and skin have very different acoustic impedances, so without gel most ultrasound would be reflected

parts.examinerComment: Answers should refer to acoustic impedance matching.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Using a Hubble constant of 2.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹, calculate the recession speed of a galaxy {d} × 10²⁴ m away, in m s⁻¹.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Use Wien's displacement law to find the peak wavelength emitted by a star with surface temperature {T} K, in m. (λmax T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K)
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A spectral line with laboratory wavelength 656 nm is observed at {lo} nm in light from a galaxy. Calculate the speed of the galaxy relative to the Earth, in m s⁻¹.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered. The line is shifted to a longer wavelength, so the galaxy is moving away.

parts.prompt: Which pair contains one scalar quantity and one vector quantity?
parts.examinerComment: Work is a scalar; acceleration is a vector. Candidates often think energy-type quantities have direction because forces are involved.

parts.prompt: The diameter of a sphere is measured with a percentage uncertainty of {p}%. What is the percentage uncertainty in the calculated volume of the sphere?
parts.examinerComment: V = (4/3)π(d/2)³, so the percentage uncertainty is multiplied by the power, 3. The constants 4/3, π and ½ have no uncertainty.

parts.prompt: What is the best estimate of the kinetic energy of an adult sprinter running at top speed?
parts.examinerComment: A mass of about 70 kg and a speed of about 10 m s⁻¹ give ½ × 70 × 10² ≈ 3500 J. Estimates should be to the nearest order of magnitude.

parts.prompt: A car accelerates uniformly from {u} m s⁻¹ to {v} m s⁻¹ in {t} s. What distance does it travel in this time?
parts.examinerComment: s = ½(u + v)t. Option C assumes the car travels at its final speed throughout; option A is the extra distance due to the acceleration only.

parts.prompt: What is represented by the area under an acceleration–time graph?
parts.examinerComment: Area = acceleration × time = change in velocity. Option D describes acceleration itself.

parts.prompt: A ball is projected from level ground with speed {u} m s⁻¹ at {th}° above the horizontal. Air resistance is negligible. What is the speed of the ball at the highest point of its path?
parts.examinerComment: At the highest point the vertical component is zero but the horizontal component, u cos θ, is unchanged. Many candidates chose zero.

parts.prompt: A ball of mass {m} kg moving horizontally at {u} m s⁻¹ hits a wall and rebounds along the same line at {v} m s⁻¹. What is the magnitude of the change in momentum of the ball?
parts.examinerComment: Momentum is a vector. Taking the initial direction as positive, Δp = m(−v) − mu, so the magnitude is m(u + v). Option A ignores the reversal of direction.

parts.prompt: A trolley of mass {m1} kg moving at {u} m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary trolley of mass {m2} kg. The trolleys stick together. What is their speed immediately after the collision?
parts.examinerComment: Total momentum is conserved: {m1} × {u} = ({m1} + {m2})v. Kinetic energy is not conserved in this inelastic collision.

parts.prompt: A skydiver is falling vertically at terminal velocity. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The air resistance on the skydiver is zero.
The resultant force on the skydiver is zero.
The acceleration of the skydiver is equal to g.
The weight of the skydiver is greater than the air resistance.

markingPoints.text: B – The resultant force on the skydiver is zero.

parts.examinerComment: At terminal velocity the drag equals the weight, so the resultant force and the acceleration are both zero.

parts.prompt: A couple consists of two parallel forces, each of magnitude {F} N, acting in opposite directions. The perpendicular distance between their lines of action is {d} m. What is the torque of the couple?
parts.examinerComment: Torque of a couple = one of the forces × the perpendicular distance between them. Option C counts the force twice.

parts.prompt: Which conditions must be satisfied for a rigid object to be in equilibrium?

options.text: resultant force zero and resultant torque zero
all the forces acting on it are equal in magnitude

markingPoints.text: C – resultant force zero and resultant torque zero

parts.examinerComment: Both conditions are needed. A couple has zero resultant force but still causes rotation.

parts.prompt: A solid object of volume {Vo} × 10⁻⁴ m³ is fully submerged in water of density 1000 kg m⁻³. What is the upthrust on the object?
parts.examinerComment: Upthrust = weight of water displaced = ρgV = 1000 × 9.81 × {Vo} × 10⁻⁴. Option B is the mass of water displaced in kg, not a force.

parts.prompt: A car moves at a constant speed of {v} m s⁻¹ against a total resistive force of {F} N. What is the useful output power of the engine?
parts.examinerComment: At constant speed the driving force equals the resistive force, and P = Fv.

parts.prompt: An object is dropped from rest from a height of {h} m. Air resistance is negligible. What is its speed just before it hits the ground?
parts.examinerComment: mgh = ½mv², so v = √(2gh). The mass is not needed. Options C and D forget the square root.

parts.prompt: A box slides down a rough slope at constant speed. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The kinetic energy of the box increases.
Gravitational potential energy is transferred to thermal energy.
The total energy of the box and its surroundings decreases.
No work is done against friction.

markingPoints.text: B – Gravitational potential energy is transferred to thermal energy.

parts.examinerComment: The speed is constant, so the kinetic energy does not change. The loss of gravitational potential energy equals the work done against friction.

parts.prompt: Two identical springs, each of spring constant {k} N m⁻¹, are connected in series. What is the spring constant of the combination?
parts.examinerComment: In series each spring carries the full load, so the total extension doubles and the spring constant halves. Option D is for springs in parallel.

parts.prompt: A spring of spring constant {k} N m⁻¹ obeys Hooke's law. It is extended by {x} m. What is the elastic potential energy stored in the spring?
parts.examinerComment: E = ½kx², the area under the force–extension graph. Option D is the force needed, not the energy.

parts.prompt: Which statement describes plastic deformation of a material?

options.text: The material returns to its original shape when the load is removed.
The material does not return to its original shape when the load is removed.

markingPoints.text: C – The material does not return to its original shape when the load is removed.

parts.examinerComment: Plastic deformation is permanent. Option D describes brittle behaviour.

parts.prompt: Vertically polarised light of intensity {I0} W m⁻² is incident on a polarising filter. The transmission axis of the filter is at {th}° to the vertical. What is the intensity of the light transmitted?
parts.examinerComment: Malus's law: I = I₀cos²θ. Option B gives the amplitude ratio applied to the intensity.

parts.prompt: Which list of electromagnetic waves is in order of increasing wavelength?

markingPoints.text: A – γ-rays, ultraviolet, infrared, radio waves

parts.examinerComment: Candidates should know the order of the principal regions and their approximate wavelengths.

parts.prompt: Two points on a progressive wave are {d} cm apart along the direction of travel. The wavelength is {lam} cm. What is the phase difference between the oscillations at the two points?
parts.examinerComment: Phase difference = (distance ÷ wavelength) × 360°. One whole wavelength corresponds to 360°, not 180°.

parts.prompt: A diffraction grating has {N} lines per millimetre. Light of wavelength {lam} nm is incident normally on it. What is the angle between the first-order maximum and the straight-through direction?
parts.examinerComment: d = 1/({N} × 10³) m and d sin θ = nλ with n = 1. Option C is the second-order angle.

parts.prompt: Which condition is necessary for two sources of waves to produce an interference pattern that is stable and observable?

options.text: The sources have the same amplitude.
The sources have a constant phase difference.
The sources are in phase with each other.
The sources are a whole number of wavelengths apart.

markingPoints.text: B – The sources have a constant phase difference.

parts.examinerComment: Coherent sources have a constant phase difference; they need not be in phase. Equal amplitudes give the best contrast but are not essential.

parts.prompt: A string of length {L} m is fixed at both ends. It vibrates at its fundamental frequency of {f} Hz. What is the speed of the waves on the string?
parts.examinerComment: At the fundamental frequency the length of the string is half a wavelength, so λ = 2L and v = fλ.

parts.prompt: The resistance of a filament lamp increases as the potential difference across it increases. What is the reason for this?

options.text: The number of free electrons in the filament decreases.
The filament gets longer as it heats up.
The lattice ions vibrate more as the temperature rises, so the electrons collide with them more often.
The current in the filament decreases.

markingPoints.text: C – The lattice ions vibrate more as the temperature rises, so the electrons collide with them more often.

parts.examinerComment: The current still increases, but less than proportionally. Answers should refer to the increased vibration of the lattice ions.

parts.prompt: An electric heater has a power of {P} W when it is connected to a {Vs} V supply. What is the resistance of the heater?
parts.examinerComment: P = V²/R, so R = V²/P. Option A is the current in amperes.

parts.prompt: The current in a metal wire is unchanged when the wire is replaced by one of the same metal with half the diameter. What happens to the drift speed of the electrons?

markingPoints.text: D – It is multiplied by four.

parts.examinerComment: I = nAvq. Halving the diameter quarters the cross-sectional area, so v increases by a factor of four.

parts.prompt: Resistors of {R1} kΩ and {R2} kΩ are connected in series across a {Vs} V supply of negligible internal resistance. What is the potential difference across the {R2} kΩ resistor?
parts.examinerComment: The p.d. divides in the ratio of the resistances: V = {Vs} × {R2}/({R1} + {R2}).

parts.prompt: Two resistors, each of resistance {R} Ω, are connected in parallel. This combination is connected in series with a third resistor of resistance {R} Ω. What is the total resistance?
parts.examinerComment: The parallel pair is {=R/2} Ω, and adding {R} Ω in series gives {=1.5*R} Ω.

parts.prompt: A battery is connected to a lamp. Why is the potential difference across the battery terminals less than the e.m.f. of the battery?

options.text: Some charge is lost inside the battery.
Energy is dissipated in the internal resistance of the battery.
The current inside the battery is smaller than in the lamp.
The lamp has a higher resistance than the battery.

markingPoints.text: B – Energy is dissipated in the internal resistance of the battery.

parts.examinerComment: Charge is conserved (option A is wrong); some of the energy per unit charge is transferred to thermal energy in the internal resistance.

parts.prompt: A nucleus of uranium-238 (proton number 92) emits an α-particle and then two β⁻ particles. What are the nucleon number and proton number of the final nucleus?
parts.examinerComment: α decay: nucleon number −4, proton number −2. Each β⁻ decay: proton number +1 and no change in nucleon number.

parts.prompt: A meson has the quark composition u d̄ (an up quark and an anti-down antiquark). What is its charge?
parts.examinerComment: u has charge +⅔e and d̄ has charge +⅓e, giving +e. Candidates must remember that antiquarks have the opposite charge.

parts.prompt: In the α-particle scattering experiment, most α-particles passed straight through a thin gold foil. What does this show?

options.text: Most of the atom is empty space.

markingPoints.text: A – Most of the atom is empty space.

parts.examinerComment: The positive charge of the nucleus is deduced from the small number of large-angle deflections, not from the particles passing straight through.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Two forces of {F1} N and {F2} N act at a point at right angles to each other. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force, in N.
parts.examinerComment: Forces are vectors and cannot simply be added. Some candidates gave {=F1+F2} N.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain the difference between a systematic error and a random error in a measurement.

markingPoints.text: B1 for a systematic error makes all readings too large or too small by the same amount / in the same direction (e.g. a zero error)
B1 for random errors cause readings to be scattered about the true value
B1 for random errors are reduced by repeating and averaging; systematic errors are not

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers gave an example of each type. Repeating readings does not remove a systematic error.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A stone is thrown vertically upwards from ground level with a speed of {u} m s⁻¹. Air resistance is negligible. Calculate the maximum height reached by the stone, in m.

markingPoints.text: C1 for v² = u² + 2as with v = 0 and a = −9.81 m s⁻²

parts.examinerComment: Most candidates used the correct equation. A few used g = 10 m s⁻², which is not accepted when 9.81 m s⁻² is given on the data sheet.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A car travels at {v} m s⁻¹. The driver sees a hazard and reacts after {tr} s. The brakes then give a uniform deceleration of {a} m s⁻². Calculate the total stopping distance from the moment the driver sees the hazard, in m.
parts.examinerComment: Many candidates forgot that the car travels at constant speed during the reaction time.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A lift of mass {m} kg is accelerated upwards at {a} m s⁻² by the tension in its cable. Calculate the tension in the cable, in N.
parts.examinerComment: Candidates who equated the tension to ma alone forgot that the weight also acts on the lift.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: State Newton's second law of motion in terms of momentum.

markingPoints.text: B1 for the resultant force is proportional to (or equal to) the rate of change of momentum
B1 for (the change in momentum is) in the direction of the resultant force

parts.examinerComment: 'Force equals mass times acceleration' was not accepted, as the question asked for a statement in terms of momentum.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A diver is at a depth of {h} m below the surface of the sea. The density of sea water is 1030 kg m⁻³ and the atmospheric pressure is 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa. Calculate the total pressure on the diver, in Pa.
parts.examinerComment: Many candidates calculated only the pressure due to the water and forgot to add atmospheric pressure.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A uniform plank of weight {W} N and length {L} m rests horizontally on two supports, one at each end. A person of weight {P} N stands on the plank {x} m from the left-hand end. Calculate the force exerted on the plank by the right-hand support, in N.

markingPoints.text: C1 for taking moments about the left-hand support

parts.examinerComment: Taking moments about one support removes the unknown force there. The weight of a uniform plank acts at its centre.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A cyclist and bicycle have a total mass of {m} kg. They free-wheel down a hill, descending a vertical height of {h} m, and their speed increases from {u} m s⁻¹ to {v} m s⁻¹. Calculate the energy dissipated by resistive forces, in J.

markingPoints.text: C1 for loss of GPE = {=round(m*9.81*h)} J
C1 for gain in KE = {=round(0.5*m*(v^2-u^2))} J

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers set out the energy changes clearly before subtracting. The kinetic energy at the start must be included.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Starting from the definition of work done, show that the change in gravitational potential energy of a mass m raised through a height Δh near the Earth's surface is mgΔh.

markingPoints.text: B1 for work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force
B1 for the force needed (at constant speed) equals the weight, mg
B1 for the distance moved in the direction of the force is Δh, so W = mgΔh, and this work is stored as GPE

parts.examinerComment: Candidates needed to state that the force is equal to the weight and that the field is uniform close to the Earth's surface.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A steel wire of length {L} m and diameter {d} mm hangs vertically and supports a load of {F} N. The Young modulus of steel is 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa. Calculate the extension of the wire, in mm.
parts.examinerComment: The most common error was using the diameter instead of the radius when calculating the area.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: State Hooke's law and explain what is meant by the elastic limit of a material.

markingPoints.text: B1 for the extension is proportional to the force (load), provided the limit of proportionality is not exceeded
B1 for the elastic limit is the maximum force (stress) beyond which the material does not return to its original length when the force is removed

parts.examinerComment: Many confused the elastic limit with the limit of proportionality. They are often close but are not the same point.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: The amplitude of a progressive wave is reduced from {A1} mm to {A2} mm. The intensity of the wave was originally {I} W m⁻². Calculate the new intensity, in W m⁻².
parts.examinerComment: Candidates who assumed intensity is proportional to amplitude scored no marks.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A source of sound moves away from a stationary observer at constant speed. Explain why the observer hears a frequency lower than the frequency emitted by the source.

markingPoints.text: B1 for successive wavefronts are emitted from positions further from the observer
B1 for so the wavelength received is longer (wavefronts are spread out)
B1 for the speed of sound is unchanged, so f = v/λ is lower

parts.examinerComment: Weaker answers said the wave 'slows down'. The speed of sound in air does not depend on the motion of the source.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Light of wavelength {lam} nm is incident normally on a diffraction grating with {N} lines per millimetre. Calculate the highest order of maximum that can be observed.

markingPoints.text: C1 for d = 1/({N} × 10³) m and sin θ ≤ 1, so n ≤ d/λ = {=round(1/(N*lam*1e-6),2)}

parts.examinerComment: The order must be a whole number and must be rounded down. Several candidates rounded {=round(1/(N*lam*1e-6),2)} up.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain how a stationary wave is formed on a stretched string fixed at both ends.

markingPoints.text: B1 for a wave travels along the string and is reflected at the fixed end
B1 for the incident and reflected waves (same frequency and speed) travel in opposite directions and superpose
B1 for nodes form where the waves always cancel and antinodes where the amplitude is a maximum

parts.examinerComment: The key words are reflection and superposition. Answers that described only the appearance of the string scored one mark at most.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A constantan wire has a diameter of {d} mm. The resistivity of constantan is 4.9 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m. Calculate the length of wire needed to make a resistor of resistance {R} Ω, in m.
parts.examinerComment: Candidates must convert the diameter to metres and halve it before squaring.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A copper wire of cross-sectional area {A} mm² carries a current of {I} A. The number of free electrons per unit volume in copper is 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³. Calculate the mean drift speed of the electrons, in m s⁻¹.
parts.examinerComment: The drift speed is very small. Answers of several metres per second should have prompted a check of the unit conversion.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A cell of e.m.f. {emf} V supplies a current of {I} A to an external resistor. The potential difference across the terminals of the cell is {=emf - I*r} V. Calculate the internal resistance of the cell, in Ω.

markingPoints.text: C1 for E = V + Ir (lost volts = {=round(I*r,2)} V)

parts.examinerComment: The difference between the e.m.f. and the terminal p.d. is the p.d. across the internal resistance.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A potential divider consists of a thermistor (negative temperature coefficient) in series with a fixed resistor, connected across a battery. The output is the potential difference across the fixed resistor. Explain what happens to the output potential difference when the temperature of the thermistor increases.

markingPoints.text: B1 for the resistance of the thermistor decreases as temperature rises
B1 for the fixed resistor now has a larger proportion of the total resistance (or the current increases)
B1 for so the output p.d. increases

parts.examinerComment: A complete answer links the change in resistance to the share of the p.d. Stating only 'the output increases' scored one mark.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A hadron is made of three quarks. Name the class of hadron to which it belongs.
parts.examinerComment: Mesons consist of a quark and an antiquark. Most candidates answered correctly.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A nucleus has proton number {Z} and nucleon number {A}. It emits an α-particle and the resulting nucleus then emits a β⁻ particle. Calculate the number of neutrons in the final nucleus.

markingPoints.text: C1 for final nucleus has nucleon number {=A-4} and proton number {=Z-1}

parts.examinerComment: In β⁻ decay a neutron changes into a proton, so the neutron number falls by one as well as the proton number rising.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Define the radian.

markingPoints.text: B1 for the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius

parts.examinerComment: Answers must mention both the arc length and the radius.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A small mass of {m} kg is attached to a string and moves in a horizontal circle of radius {r} m on a smooth table. The frequency of rotation is {f} Hz. Calculate the tension in the string, in N.
parts.examinerComment: The tension provides the centripetal force. Many candidates used the frequency instead of the angular speed.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A car travels over the top of a hump-backed bridge. The top of the bridge is part of a vertical circle of radius {r} m. Calculate the maximum speed at which the car can pass over the top without losing contact with the road, in m s⁻¹.

markingPoints.text: C1 for mg = mv²/r when the contact force is zero

parts.examinerComment: Good answers explained that the contact force becomes zero when the weight alone provides the centripetal force.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: In a centrifuge, a sample {r} cm from the axis of rotation has a centripetal acceleration of {n} g, where g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the rate of rotation of the centrifuge, in revolutions per minute.

markingPoints.text: C1 for a = ω²r with a = {=n*9.81} m s⁻²

parts.examinerComment: Converting the radius to metres and the angular speed to revolutions per minute were both needed.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: A ball on a string is swung in a vertical circle. Explain why the tension in the string is greater when the ball is at the bottom of the circle than when it is at the top.

markingPoints.text: B1 for the resultant force towards the centre provides the centripetal force mv²/r
B1 for at the bottom T − mg = mv²/r but at the top T + mg = mv²/r
B1 for the speed is also greater at the bottom (GPE converted to KE), so the required centripetal force is greater

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers wrote an equation for each position. The weight acts towards the centre at the top but away from it at the bottom.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Two lead spheres of masses {m1} kg and {m2} kg have their centres {r} m apart. Calculate the gravitational force between them, in N.
parts.examinerComment: The force is extremely small, which explains why gravitational attraction between everyday objects is not noticed.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A planet has mass {M} × 10²³ kg and radius {R} × 10⁶ m. Calculate the gravitational field strength at its surface, in N kg⁻¹.
parts.examinerComment: Errors in handling powers of ten were common. Candidates should check that the answer is sensible compared with 9.81 N kg⁻¹.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A moon has mass {M} × 10²² kg and radius {R} × 10⁶ m. Calculate the gravitational potential at its surface, in J kg⁻¹.
parts.examinerComment: The negative sign is required: the potential is zero at infinity and work must be done to move a mass away from the moon.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: A satellite is in a circular orbit {h} km above the surface of the Earth. The Earth has mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m. Calculate the orbital speed of the satellite, in m s⁻¹.
parts.examinerComment: The orbital radius is measured from the centre of the Earth. Many candidates used the height above the surface.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Explain why a geostationary satellite must orbit above the equator, moving from west to east, with a period of 24 hours.

markingPoints.text: B1 for it must stay above the same point on the Earth's surface
B1 for it must rotate in the same direction as the Earth (west to east) with the same period as the Earth's rotation, 24 hours
B1 for the centre of the orbit must be the centre of the Earth (gravitational force towards the centre), so only an equatorial orbit stays over one point

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates gave the conditions without explaining why each was needed.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain what is meant when two objects are said to be in thermal equilibrium.

markingPoints.text: B1 for there is no net transfer of thermal energy between them
B1 for they are at the same temperature

parts.examinerComment: Saying 'no heat flows' is not enough: energy is exchanged, but there is no net transfer.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: {m1} kg of water at {T1} °C is mixed with {m2} kg of water at {T2} °C in an insulated container. Calculate the final temperature of the mixture, in °C.

markingPoints.text: C1 for energy lost by hot water = energy gained by cold water: {m1} × c × ({T1} − θ) = {m2} × c × (θ − {T2})

parts.examinerComment: The specific heat capacity cancels, so it is not needed. Some candidates simply averaged the two temperatures.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A block of metal of mass {m} kg is heated by a {P} W electrical heater for {t} s. Its temperature rises by {=round(P*t/(m*c),1)} K. Assuming no energy is lost, calculate the specific heat capacity of the metal, in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
parts.examinerComment: In practice energy losses mean the experimental value is higher than the true value.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Water in a kettle is kept boiling by a {P} W heater. In {t} s the mass of water decreases by {=round(P*t/2260,1)} g. Assuming all the energy supplied is used to vaporise the water, calculate the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water, in J kg⁻¹.

markingPoints.text: C1 for Pt = mL with m in kg

parts.examinerComment: The mass must be converted from grams to kilograms.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Name one physical property of a substance that varies with temperature and can be used to measure temperature.
acceptedAnswers: the resistance of a metal wire
pressure of a gas at constant volume

markingPoints.text: B1 for any suitable property, e.g. resistance, volume of a liquid, pressure of a gas at constant volume, e.m.f. of a thermocouple

parts.examinerComment: Most candidates gave a correct property. 'Heat' is not a physical property.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A sealed rigid container holds gas at {T1} °C and a pressure of {p1} × 10⁵ Pa. The gas is heated to {T2} °C. Calculate the new pressure, in Pa.

markingPoints.text: C1 for p/T constant with T in kelvin

parts.examinerComment: Using Celsius temperatures was the most common error and gave a much larger answer.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A nitrogen molecule has mass 4.65 × 10⁻²⁶ kg. Calculate the root-mean-square speed of nitrogen molecules at a temperature of {T} K, in m s⁻¹.
parts.examinerComment: Candidates must take the square root of the mean square speed.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A gas at a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of {T} K occupies a volume of {Vg} m³. Calculate the number of molecules of gas, N.
parts.examinerComment: Candidates who used R found the amount in moles and needed to multiply by the Avogadro constant.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Use the kinetic model of a gas to explain how a gas exerts a pressure on the walls of its container.

markingPoints.text: B1 for molecules collide with the walls and rebound, so their momentum changes
B1 for the wall exerts a force on each molecule equal to its rate of change of momentum, so (Newton's third law) the molecules exert a force on the wall
B1 for many collisions per second give a steady average force, and pressure = force ÷ area

parts.examinerComment: The best answers used the idea of change in momentum explicitly rather than just 'molecules hit the walls'.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: State what is meant by an ideal gas.

markingPoints.text: B1 for a gas that obeys pV ∝ T (pV = nRT)
B1 for at all pressures, volumes and temperatures (T in kelvin)

parts.examinerComment: Both parts were needed. Listing the kinetic theory assumptions did not answer the question.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A gas is compressed. {W} J of work is done on the gas and the gas transfers {Q} J of thermal energy to its surroundings. Calculate the change in internal energy of the gas, in J. Give a negative value for a decrease.

markingPoints.text: C1 for ΔU = q + W with q = −{Q} J and W = +{W} J

parts.examinerComment: Candidates should state the sign convention they use. Work done on the gas is positive.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A gas is heated at a constant pressure of {p} × 10⁵ Pa. Its volume increases from {V1} × 10⁻³ m³ to {=V1+dV} × 10⁻³ m³ and it is supplied with {Q} J of thermal energy. Calculate the increase in internal energy of the gas, in J.

markingPoints.text: C1 for work done by the gas = pΔV = {=round(p*100*dV)} J
C1 for ΔU = q + W with W negative

parts.examinerComment: Work done by the gas is energy leaving the system, so it is subtracted from the heat supplied.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain why the internal energy of an ideal gas is directly proportional to its thermodynamic temperature.

markingPoints.text: B1 for there are no intermolecular forces, so the molecules have no potential energy
B1 for internal energy is the total random kinetic energy, and the mean kinetic energy is proportional to T

parts.examinerComment: Many answers mentioned kinetic energy but did not explain why potential energy is zero.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: State the first law of thermodynamics as an equation, explaining the meaning of each term and the sign convention used.

markingPoints.text: B1 for ΔU is the increase in internal energy
B1 for q is the thermal energy supplied to the system and W is the work done on the system

parts.examinerComment: Stating 'work done' without saying whether it is done on or by the system lost the final mark.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: A gas expands so quickly that there is no time for any thermal energy to be transferred to or from it. State whether the temperature of the gas increases, decreases or stays the same.

markingPoints.text: B1 for decreases (the gas does work, q = 0, so ΔU is negative)

parts.examinerComment: Since q = 0 and the gas does work on its surroundings, its internal energy and therefore its temperature fall.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: An object oscillates with simple harmonic motion of frequency {f} Hz and amplitude {A} cm. Calculate the maximum acceleration of the object, in m s⁻².

markingPoints.text: C1 for a = ω²x₀ with ω = 2πf

parts.examinerComment: The maximum acceleration occurs at maximum displacement.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: An object oscillates with simple harmonic motion of amplitude {x0} cm and angular frequency {w} rad s⁻¹. Calculate the speed of the object when its displacement is {x} cm, in m s⁻¹.
parts.examinerComment: Some candidates subtracted the displacement from the amplitude before squaring.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A mass of {m} kg oscillates with simple harmonic motion of frequency {f} Hz and amplitude {x0} cm. Calculate the total energy of the oscillation, in J.
parts.examinerComment: The total energy equals the maximum kinetic energy. The amplitude must be in metres.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: A system is forced to oscillate. Describe how the graph of amplitude against driving frequency changes when the degree of damping is increased.

markingPoints.text: B1 for the peak amplitude is lower at all frequencies
B1 for the peak becomes broader / flatter
B1 for the frequency at maximum amplitude shifts to a slightly lower value

parts.examinerComment: Most candidates knew the amplitude falls. Fewer mentioned the broadening and the shift of the peak.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Distinguish between light damping, critical damping and heavy damping.

markingPoints.text: B1 for light damping: the system oscillates with gradually decreasing amplitude
B1 for critical damping: the system returns to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating
B1 for heavy damping: the system returns to equilibrium slowly without oscillating

parts.examinerComment: Each type should be described in terms of oscillation and the time taken to return to equilibrium.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A charged oil drop of mass {m} × 10⁻¹⁵ kg is held stationary between two horizontal metal plates {d} mm apart. The potential difference between the plates is {=round(m*1e-15*9.81*d*1e-3/(n*1.6e-19))} V. Calculate the charge on the oil drop, in C.
parts.examinerComment: The electric force must be equal and opposite to the weight. Good candidates noticed that the answer is a whole-number multiple of e.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A small isolated sphere carries a charge of +{Q} nC. Calculate the electric potential at a distance of {r} m from the centre of the sphere, in V.
parts.examinerComment: Some candidates used r² and calculated the field strength instead of the potential.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: An electron is in a uniform electric field of strength {Ef} × 10⁴ V m⁻¹. Calculate the magnitude of its acceleration, in m s⁻².

markingPoints.text: C1 for F = eE and a = F/m

parts.examinerComment: The gravitational force on the electron is negligible compared with the electric force.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Define electric potential at a point.

markingPoints.text: B1 for work done per unit positive charge
B1 for in bringing a small test charge from infinity to the point

parts.examinerComment: 'Energy per unit charge' without reference to infinity scored one mark.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: A charge of +{q} μC is moved from a point where the electric potential is {V1} V to a point where the potential is {V2} V. Calculate the work done on the charge, in J.

markingPoints.text: C1 for W = QΔV with ΔV = {=V2-V1} V

parts.examinerComment: Work must be done on a positive charge to move it to a higher potential.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A {C1} μF capacitor is connected in series with a {C2} μF capacitor. Calculate the combined capacitance, in μF.
parts.examinerComment: The combined capacitance in series is less than the smaller capacitance. Candidates who added the values used the rule for parallel capacitors.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A {C} μF capacitor is charged to {V0} V and then discharged through a {R} kΩ resistor. Calculate the potential difference across the capacitor {=k*R*C/1000} s after the discharge starts, in V.
parts.examinerComment: Most candidates used the exponential equation correctly. The time constant must be calculated with C in farads and R in ohms.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A {C} μF capacitor discharges through a {R} kΩ resistor. Calculate the time taken for the charge on the capacitor to fall to half its initial value, in s.
parts.examinerComment: Candidates who wrote ½ = e^(−t/RC) and took natural logarithms usually succeeded.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Define capacitance.

markingPoints.text: B1 for charge stored per unit potential difference (C = Q/V)
B1 for charge on one plate / of one sign, and p.d. between the plates

parts.examinerComment: A word equation is acceptable provided the quantities are identified correctly.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: A capacitor is charged by a battery. Explain why the energy stored in the capacitor is ½QV and not QV, where Q is the final charge and V the final potential difference.

markingPoints.text: B1 for as charge is added, the p.d. across the capacitor increases from zero to V (p.d. ∝ charge)
B1 for the energy stored is the area under the p.d.–charge graph, a triangle of area ½QV

parts.examinerComment: QV is the energy supplied by the battery; half of it is dissipated in the resistance of the circuit.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Positive ions pass undeflected through a region where a uniform electric field of strength {Ef} × 10³ V m⁻¹ is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of flux density {B} T. Calculate the speed of the ions, in m s⁻¹.
parts.examinerComment: The charge cancels, so ions of any charge with this speed pass undeflected.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A slice of semiconductor of thickness {t} mm carries a current of {I} mA. A magnetic field of flux density {B} T acts perpendicular to the slice. The number density of charge carriers is 2.0 × 10²³ m⁻³. Calculate the Hall voltage, in mV.

markingPoints.text: C1 for correct conversion of mA and mm

parts.examinerComment: The Hall voltage in a semiconductor is much larger than in a metal because n is much smaller.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: An aircraft with a wingspan of {L} m flies horizontally at {v} m s⁻¹. The vertical component of the Earth's magnetic field is {B} × 10⁻⁵ T. Calculate the e.m.f. induced between the wing tips, in V.

markingPoints.text: C1 for E = BLv (rate of cutting flux)

parts.examinerComment: Only the vertical component of the field is cut by horizontal wings.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: State Lenz's law and explain how it is consistent with the conservation of energy.

markingPoints.text: B1 for the direction of the induced e.m.f. (current) is such as to oppose the change that produces it
B1 for work must therefore be done (against the opposing force) to produce the induced current
B1 for this work is the source of the electrical energy; if the effect aided the change, energy would be created

parts.examinerComment: Candidates should refer to the induced e.m.f. or current opposing the change in flux linkage, not opposing the field.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: State the SI unit of magnetic flux.

markingPoints.text: B1 for weber (Wb) or T m²

parts.examinerComment: The tesla is the unit of magnetic flux density, not of flux.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: An alternating current is given by I = {I0} sin({w}t), where I is in amperes and t in seconds. Calculate the r.m.s. value of the current, in A.
parts.examinerComment: The r.m.s. value is the peak value divided by √2.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: An alternating current is given by I = {I0} sin({w}t), where I is in amperes and t in seconds. Calculate the frequency of the current, in Hz.
parts.examinerComment: The number multiplying t is the angular frequency, not the frequency.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A lamp is rated at {P} W when connected to an alternating supply of r.m.s. voltage {Vr} V. Calculate the peak current in the lamp, in A.
parts.examinerComment: Power ratings for a.c. supplies use r.m.s. values.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Distinguish between half-wave rectification and full-wave rectification of an alternating voltage.

markingPoints.text: B1 for half-wave: only one half of each cycle is passed; the output is zero for the other half (one diode)
B1 for full-wave: both halves of each cycle give output in the same direction (e.g. using four diodes in a bridge)

parts.examinerComment: Diagrams were not required, but answers had to make clear what happens in each half-cycle.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Define the root-mean-square (r.m.s.) value of an alternating current.

markingPoints.text: B1 for the value of the steady (direct) current
B1 for that produces the same (mean) power in a resistor

parts.examinerComment: Many described how to calculate the r.m.s. value instead of defining it.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A metal surface has a work function of {W0} eV. Calculate the threshold frequency for photoelectric emission from this surface, in Hz.

markingPoints.text: C1 for Φ = hf₀ with Φ converted to joules

parts.examinerComment: The work function must be converted from electronvolts to joules.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A laser emits light of wavelength {lam} nm with a power of {P} mW. Calculate the number of photons emitted per second.
parts.examinerComment: Many candidates forgot to convert milliwatts to watts.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: An electron in an atom moves from an energy level of −{U} eV to an energy level of −{L} eV. Calculate the wavelength of the photon emitted, in m.
parts.examinerComment: The energy of the photon equals the difference between the two levels, not the value of either level.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain how the photoelectric effect provides evidence for the particulate nature of electromagnetic radiation.

markingPoints.text: B1 for there is a threshold frequency below which no electrons are emitted, however intense the radiation
B1 for the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons depends on frequency but not on intensity
B1 for emission is instantaneous / one photon gives all its energy to one electron, which a wave model cannot explain

parts.examinerComment: The best answers explained why each observation cannot be explained by the wave theory.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Describe evidence that electrons can behave as waves.

markingPoints.text: B1 for electrons passing through a thin layer of graphite (crystal) produce a diffraction pattern of rings
B1 for diffraction is a wave property; the de Broglie wavelength is similar to the atomic spacing

parts.examinerComment: Candidates needed to name diffraction as the wave behaviour shown.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A sample contains {N} × 10²⁰ nuclei of a radioactive isotope with a half-life of {T} hours. Calculate the activity of the sample, in Bq.

markingPoints.text: C1 for λ = ln 2 / t½ with t½ in seconds

parts.examinerComment: The half-life must be converted to seconds to give an activity in becquerels.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A radioactive source has an initial activity of {A0} kBq and a half-life of {T} days. Calculate its activity after {t} days, in kBq.

markingPoints.text: C1 for A = A₀e^(−λt) with λ = ln 2 / {T}

parts.examinerComment: When the time is not a whole number of half-lives the exponential equation must be used.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A helium-4 nucleus has a mass of 4.001 506 u. The mass of a proton is 1.007 276 u and the mass of a neutron is 1.008 665 u. Calculate the binding energy per nucleon of helium-4, in MeV.

markingPoints.text: C1 for E = Δmc² = 4.54 × 10⁻¹² J (28.4 MeV)

parts.examinerComment: Candidates must divide the binding energy by the nucleon number, 4.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: With reference to the variation of binding energy per nucleon with nucleon number, explain why energy is released when a heavy nucleus undergoes fission.

markingPoints.text: B1 for binding energy per nucleon is a maximum near iron (A ≈ 56) and decreases for heavier nuclei
B1 for the fission fragments have a higher binding energy per nucleon than the original nucleus
B1 for so the total binding energy increases and the mass of the products is less; the mass difference is released as energy

parts.examinerComment: Weaker answers said that 'energy is released when bonds are broken', which is incorrect.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Explain what is meant by saying that radioactive decay is both random and spontaneous.

markingPoints.text: B1 for random: it is not possible to predict which nucleus will decay next or when a particular nucleus will decay
B1 for spontaneous: the decay is not affected by external factors such as temperature or pressure

parts.examinerComment: Both terms needed a separate explanation.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: The specific acoustic impedance of fat is {Z1} × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹ and that of muscle is {Z2} × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹. Calculate the intensity reflection coefficient for ultrasound at a fat–muscle boundary.
parts.examinerComment: Most of the ultrasound is transmitted at a boundary between two soft tissues, which is why deeper structures can be imaged.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: In PET scanning, a positron annihilates with an electron, producing two γ-ray photons. Both particles are effectively at rest before the annihilation. Calculate the energy of each γ-ray photon, in J.

markingPoints.text: C1 for total energy = 2mₑc² shared between two photons, so each photon has mₑc²

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates doubled the energy. Each photon carries the rest energy of one particle.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: An ultrasound pulse is reflected from a boundary inside the body. The echo is received {t} μs after the pulse is emitted. The speed of ultrasound in tissue is 1540 m s⁻¹. Calculate the depth of the boundary below the transducer, in cm.

markingPoints.text: C1 for distance travelled = speed × time, and depth = half of this

parts.examinerComment: The pulse travels to the boundary and back, so the distance must be halved.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain how a piezoelectric transducer produces ultrasound.

markingPoints.text: B1 for an alternating p.d. is applied across the piezoelectric crystal
B1 for the crystal changes shape (expands and contracts) as the p.d. changes, so it vibrates
B1 for the p.d. has an ultrasonic frequency equal to the natural frequency of the crystal, so it resonates and emits ultrasound waves

parts.examinerComment: Candidates should refer to the change of shape of the crystal and to resonance.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Explain how the contrast of an X-ray image of soft tissue, such as the stomach, can be improved.

markingPoints.text: B1 for use a contrast medium such as barium (meal) or iodine
B1 for it has a high attenuation coefficient (high proton number), so it absorbs X-rays much more than the surrounding tissue

parts.examinerComment: Answers needed to explain why the contrast medium increases the difference in attenuation.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: The radiant flux intensity at the Earth from a star is {F} × 10⁻⁹ W m⁻². The star is {d} × 10¹⁷ m from the Earth. Calculate the luminosity of the star, in W.
parts.examinerComment: The inverse square law applies because the radiation spreads out uniformly over a sphere.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A star has a luminosity of {L} × 10²⁶ W and a surface temperature of {T} K. Calculate the radius of the star, in m.

markingPoints.text: C1 for correct rearrangement for r

parts.examinerComment: The temperature must be raised to the fourth power. Some candidates forgot to take the square root at the end.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: The Hubble constant is {H} × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. Use it to estimate the age of the Universe, in years. (1 year = 3.16 × 10⁷ s)
parts.examinerComment: This estimate assumes that galaxies have always receded at their present speeds.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain what is meant by a standard candle.

markingPoints.text: B1 for an astronomical object of known luminosity
B1 for so its distance can be found by measuring its radiant flux intensity at the Earth (inverse square law)

parts.examinerComment: Examples such as Cepheid variable stars or type 1a supernovae were credited only with an explanation.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Explain how observations of the light from distant galaxies support the Big Bang theory.

markingPoints.text: B1 for the light from distant galaxies is redshifted (spectral lines at longer wavelengths)
B1 for so the galaxies are receding, and recession speed is proportional to distance (Hubble's law)
B1 for so the Universe is expanding, suggesting it began from a single point (very small, hot and dense) in the past

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers linked redshift to recession, Hubble's law to expansion and expansion to an origin at a single point.
